items.title: Pudu expands beyond service robots into semi-humanoids and quadrupeds
items.summary: Pudu Robotics is expanding its focus beyond service robots into developing semi-humanoids and quadrupeds. At IFA 2026, the company exhibited robots including the industrial semi-humanoid D7 and the quadruped D5-W. The D7 concentrates its joints in the arms, waist, and head, demonstrating an alternative approach to humanoid design for industrial tasks. The D5-W robot can navigate uneven terrain and autonomously recover from falls, combining wheeled and legged locomotion. Pudu is also increasing autonomy in its existing commercial robotics, as seen with its self-evaluating cleaning robot.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, Pudu expands beyond service robots into semi-humanoids and quadrupeds. This report details the company's development of advanced robotic platforms including semi-humanoids and quadrupeds showcased at the IFA 2026 exhibition. At the event, Pudu displayed the industrial semi-humanoid D7 and the quadruped D5-W robot. The D7 features its primary joint concentration in the arms, waist, and head, presenting a design alternative for industrial applications. The D5-W robot integrates both wheeled and legged locomotion, enabling navigation over uneven terrain and autonomous recovery from falls. Furthermore, Pudu is enhancing the autonomy of its current commercial robotics, demonstrated by the self-evaluating cleaning robot. This development signals a shift in robotic design toward more complex, versatile physical forms.

items.title: Tesla patent reveals touch-sensitive skin for robot hands
items.summary: Tesla filed a US patent for a touch-sensitive "skin" to mold around robot fingers and palms for detecting contact, force, and pressure. The technology involves printing tactile sensors onto flexible materials and then heat-forming them into three-dimensional shapes. These sensors function by overlapping conductive regions on flexible substrates, detecting pressure changes via capacitive and piezoresistive methods. The patent emphasizes manufacturability using techniques like screen printing and thermoforming for scalable production. This innovation aims to give humanoid robots more dexterous manipulation capabilities by allowing them to sense how firmly they are holding objects.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, "Tesla patent reveals touch-sensitive skin for robot hands". This report details a US patent filed by Tesla for a touch-sensitive skin designed for robot hands, which allows for the detection of contact, force, and pressure. The technology involves printing tactile sensors onto flexible materials and subsequently heat-forming them into three-dimensional shapes. These sensors operate by utilizing overlapping conductive regions on flexible substrates to detect pressure changes through capacitive and piezoresistive methods. The patent further emphasizes manufacturability through techniques such as screen printing and thermoforming to facilitate scalable production of this material. This innovation seeks to enhance humanoid robots' dexterity by providing them with sensory feedback regarding object manipulation. The development indicates a progression toward more sophisticated tactile sensing in robotic systems.

items.title: Skild AI trains robots to learn physical skills through self-play
items.summary: Skild AI developed a self-play training method for robots to learn physical skills without human demonstrations, using its S1 robotics foundation model. Robots learned soccer skills through self-play against increasingly capable versions of themselves in a simulated environment. This process allowed the robots to autonomously develop complex physical behaviors like dribbling and tackling based on the objective of scoring. The learned policy was successfully transferred to a physical humanoid robot, demonstrating the potential for physical AGI. This approach aims to reduce the reliance on human demonstration data for teaching robots complex physical tasks.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, "Skild AI trains robots to learn physical skills through self-play". This report details a self-play training method developed by Skild AI that enables robots to acquire physical skills without requiring human demonstrations. The key finding is that robots autonomously learned complex physical behaviors, such as soccer skills, by playing against increasingly capable versions of themselves within a simulated environment. This process allowed the robots to develop intricate physical actions like dribbling and tackling based solely on the objective of scoring. The learned policy was subsequently successfully transferred to a physical humanoid robot, indicating potential for physical artificial general intelligence. This methodology seeks to decrease the dependence on human demonstration data for teaching robots complex physical tasks. The development suggests a pathway toward more autonomous physical skill acquisition in robotics.

items.title: ETH Zurich scientists turn WUJI robotic hand into self-propelled mobile manipulator
items.summary: ETH Zurich scientists transformed a WUJI robotic hand into a self-propelled mobile manipulator. The research enabled the hand to crawl, recover from falls, and move independently using its fingers for locomotion. This system functions as a "compact mobile manipulator" by eliminating the need for a separate mobility mechanism. Reinforcement learning was used to develop these locomotion skills, considering the unique characteristics of each finger. The work demonstrates an approach where the hand itself performs both locomotion and manipulation.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, ETH Zurich scientists turn WUJI robotic hand into self-propelled mobile manipulator. This report details the transformation of a WUJI robotic hand into a self-propelled mobile manipulator capable of independent locomotion. The research achieved this by enabling the hand to crawl, recover from falls, and move autonomously using its fingers for propulsion, functioning as a compact mobile manipulator without an external mobility mechanism. Reinforcement learning was the methodology employed to develop these locomotion skills by considering the unique characteristics of each finger. The system demonstrates that the manipulator itself can execute both locomotion and manipulation functions simultaneously. This work indicates progress toward integrated, self-sufficient robotic systems in the field of artificial intelligence and robotics.

items.title: Robot Talk Episode 166 – Evolving robot bodies and brains, with Rika Antonova
items.summary: Claire discussed using artificial intelligence to develop complementary robot hardware and algorithms with Rika Antonova from the University of Cambridge. Antonova is an Associate Professor whose research focuses on co-design, automated algorithm discovery, and data-efficient reinforcement learning in robotics. She has a strong background including a PhD and a Computing Innovation Fellowship from Stanford University. The Robot Talk podcast explores the world of robotics, AI, and autonomous machines weekly. This episode highlights the evolving development of robot bodies and brains.

items.title: PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims
items.summary: PNDbotics' full-size Adam humanoid has demonstrated the ability to climb onto a one-meter-high box. This movement involved analyzing the obstacle, planning movements, and placing one foot on top before transferring its weight. The climb required coordinated movement across the robot's body to support and raise itself while maintaining balance. The sequence described emphasizes obstacle analysis and movement planning preceding the actual foot placement. This capability was reported by Space and Technology based on a LinkedIn post.
items.audio_script: From Humanoid.guide, "PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims". This report details an achievement by the PNDbotics Adam humanoid demonstrating the ability to ascend a one-meter high box. The movement involved analyzing the obstacle, planning movements, and executing a sequence where one foot was placed on top before weight transfer. This climb necessitated coordinated movement across the robot's body to support and elevate itself while maintaining equilibrium. The sequence highlighted the preceding analysis of the obstacle and the planning of the movements before actual foot placement occurred. This capability was communicated via a post on LinkedIn by Space and Technology. The demonstration indicates advancements in real-world problem-solving for advanced artificial intelligence systems. Further testing of such locomotion skills is anticipated in the robotics sector.

items.title: Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route
items.summary: Waymo is launching its fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, aiming for first riders in 2028 by investing in local infrastructure and jobs. The rollout will begin with a phased, safety-first approach involving high-definition mapping and testing with autonomous specialists in Toronto's driving conditions. The expansion involves a partnership with Element Fleet Management to provide end-to-end fleet management and create numerous employment opportunities. Waymo's autonomous vehicles have demonstrated significantly lower crash rates compared to human drivers based on data from over 400 million autonomous kilometers. The service also emphasizes safety and accessibility through collaborations with various mobility advocacy organizations.

items.title: The Sequence Robotics - Issue #952: One Brain, Many Bodies: Inside Skild AI's Robotics Bet
items.summary: Skild AI is betting that robotic intelligence should be transferable across different hardware instead of being rebuilt for each machine. Their research focuses on motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this transferability. The core idea is to separate intelligence from the physical machine it inhabits. The company is testing whether these capabilities can survive the real-world demands of speed, reliability, and safety in deployment. This approach aims for the model to learn how to understand a body rather than requiring engineers to perfectly specify every physical detail beforehand.
items.audio_script: From thesequence.substack.com, The Sequence Robotics - Issue 952: One Brain, Many Bodies: Inside Skild AI's Robotics Bet details Skild AI's research into transferring robotic intelligence across different hardware. This research focuses on motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this intelligence transferability. The core concept involves separating intelligence from the physical machine, testing whether these capabilities can withstand real-world requirements for speed, reliability, and safety in deployment. The methodology involves training models to learn how to understand a body rather than requiring explicit specification of every physical detail upfront. The company is testing the viability of this approach by pushing the learned skills into physical systems. This development suggests a shift toward more adaptable and generalized artificial intelligence systems in robotics.

items.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
items.summary: Multi-dimensional featurizers are investigated to improve control over robot behavior in foundation models. Block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) are used to recover multi-dimensional features relevant to perception, language, and control. Fine-grained steering experiments show that manipulating these features predictably alters downstream action predictions. Feature-based data attribution allows for identifying minimal training data tokens necessary to remove specific behaviors. Ultimately, aligning featurizers with representation geometry offers more effective means to understand and modify robot behavior.

items.title: Navigation by Skylight Polarization via Rayleigh Model Optimization on a Road Vehicle
items.summary: The method estimates vehicle heading by optimizing a Rayleigh sky model using measurements from a division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera. This framework incorporates a pinhole camera model, a single-scattering Rayleigh polarization model, and a solar position algorithm to synthesize polarization angle information. A polarization-weighted root mean square error function is used to compare measured and simulated polarization patterns, effectively handling occlusions. Experimental results demonstrated sub-degree RMS yaw errors of $0.718^{\circ}$ to $0.889^{\circ}$ across road vehicle trajectories. The approach significantly reduces RMS heading error by up to 87% compared to other navigation methods.

items.title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception
items.summary: The research establishes feasibility ceilings for drone-mesh interception tasks before any learning policy is applied. It provides closed-form bounds for performance based on the spread and timing of agents covering a predicted arrival point. The analysis reveals that naive area ratios underestimate coverage, and optimal packing arrangements are hexagonal. Analytic placement achieves 85% of configuration performance, while learning methods achieve significantly less. These ceilings should be determined and cited before any learning experiment.

items.title: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery Improves Final Gait Selection after Irreversible Leg Damage
items.summary: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery (PGRR) is a method designed to improve gait selection after irreversible leg damage in robotics. This approach predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait executions and uses uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched tasks involving leg amputation, fracture, and joint lock, PGRR yielded a 0.106 improvement in final quality and a 0.044 improvement in slot-averaged recovery quality compared to a baseline. Furthermore, PGRR reduced low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points across all damage classes. The study indicates that conservative uncertainty handling is the key factor driving these observed performance gains.

items.title: Clarity-Driven Adaptive Mission Planning for a Solar-Powered Autonomous Surface Vessel
items.summary: The methodology employs a clarity-driven ergodic search to plan missions for solar-powered autonomous surface vessels. This approach maximizes information gathering by linking clarity to differential entropy, accounting for limitations imposed by renewable power. The system adapts an online target clarity map based on in-situ measurements to prioritize areas of interest. An ergodic path planner continuously re-plans routes considering this clarity map and the ASV's speed constraints. Simulations at Jordan Lake demonstrated the effectiveness of this method for scientific missions.

items.title: Race to Recovery: Designing Advanced Safety Systems for Autonomous Driving via Learning Autonomous Racing
items.summary: Existing safety systems fail to recover autonomous vehicles from loss-of-control situations like icing or hydroplaning because they focus on prevention rather than recovery. The research trains a racing policy using reinforcement learning to learn drifting as a time-optimal maneuver. This policy is then adapted through continued training to focus on recovery with a minimum-time reward. The transferred policy significantly improves recovery performance over existing methods, outperforming model predictive controllers. When deployed on a physical vehicle, the policy successfully recovers from states where other baselines fail.

items.title: Optimally Trading Energy for Information through Speed Trajectory Optimization of Sustainably Powered Mobile Robots
items.summary: Sustainably powered mobile robots need to optimize energy allocation to maximize information quality during long-duration missions. The study formulates this as a persistent optimal control problem involving a robot traversing a fixed closed path. The optimization uses the information-theoretic quantity of clarity as a metric to derive necessary conditions for optimal control. The research characterizes the nature of optimal control and establishes a high-speed information limit when energy is abundant. Simulation results, based on salinity characterization in the Chesapeake Bay, demonstrate the practical value of these speed trajectory optimizations.

items.title: BubbleCBF: Constructive Safety for Second-Order Systems and Application to Autonomous Robot Navigation in Unknown Environments
items.summary: The research develops a constructive method called BubbleCBF for designing feasible safety constraints for systems with second-order dynamics. This involves constructing collision-free spheres, or "bubbles," from a signed distance function to define velocity-dependent safety constraints. A quadratic-program safety filter is used to enforce the safe set, proving the resulting controller is well-defined and forward invariant under mild assumptions. The method is demonstrated by applying BubbleCBF to a differential-drive robot for safe autonomous navigation in unknown environments. This work successfully applies the framework to achieve safe navigation for mobile robots.
